dataset: Wikipedia ego network: Satyendra Nath Bose

ego.name: Satyendra Nath Bose
ego.summary: Satyendra Nath Bose was an Indian theoretical physicist, mathematician, and educator whose 1924 work on the statistics of indistinguishable light quanta initiated Bose-Einstein statistics. He developed physics teaching and research at the universities of Dhaka and Calcutta and was a leading figure in Indian science.

connections.relationship_description: Bose's father was an accountant in the East Indian Railways Engineering Department and headed the household in which Bose was raised.
connections.notes: Bose was the only son of Surendra Nath Bose and Amodini Debi.

connections.relationship_description: Bose's mother raised him in a Bengali Kayastha family in Calcutta, where he was the eldest of seven children.
connections.notes: Her name is also styled as Smt. Amodini Debi in the source.

connections.relationship_description: Saha was Bose's fellow student and long-running scientific collaborator; they translated relativity papers into English and published joint work in theoretical physics and mathematics.
shared_activities: study at Presidency College and Rajabazar Science College
translation of The Principle of Relativity in 1919
equation of state for real gases
connections.notes: Their early translation made foundational relativity work more accessible to English-reading students and scientists in India.

connections.relationship_description: Jagadish Chandra Bose was among Bose's teachers at Presidency College and was one of the scientific educators who inspired his ambitions.
connections.notes: They shared a surname but were not identified in the supplied material as close relatives.

connections.relationship_description: Ray was one of Bose's teachers at Presidency College and helped provide the high-level scientific environment of Bose's undergraduate education.
Mukherjee founded the University of Calcutta Science College that Bose entered for his master's work and later supported the research-centered university environment in which Bose began his career.
shared_activities: postgraduate mathematics and early research in relativity
connections.notes: Mukherjee's institutional leadership made the new Science College an important setting for Bose's transition from student to research scholar.

connections.relationship_description: Bose married Ushabati Ghosh in 1914; they remained married until his death and had nine children, seven of whom survived childhood.
connections.notes: Ushabati was the daughter of a prominent Calcutta physician and survived Bose.

connections.relationship_description: Einstein translated Bose's 1924 paper into German, secured its publication, and later recommended him for the Dhaka professorship. Their exchange carried Bose's work from Dhaka into the center of quantum theory.
shared_activities: English translation of Einstein's relativity work
publication of Planck's Law and the Hypothesis of Light Quanta
connections.notes: Their first connection followed Bose and Saha's request to translate Einstein's relativity papers; their decisive scientific exchange began in 1924.

connections.relationship_description: During Bose's 1924–1926 European research stay, he worked alongside de Broglie in the Paris scientific milieu of X-ray and crystallography research.
shared_activities: X-ray and crystallography work in Paris
connections.notes: This collaboration was enabled by the recognition Bose received after Einstein arranged publication of his 1924 paper.

connections.relationship_description: During Bose's 1924–1926 European research stay, he worked in Curie's laboratory environment and gained experience in X-ray and crystallography research.
shared_activities: X-ray and crystallography work in Paris
connections.notes: The supplied account identifies Curie as one of the scientists with whom Bose worked during his European stay.

connections.relationship_description: Debendra Mohan Bose gave Satyendra Nath Bose Max Planck's books Thermodynamik and Warmestrahlung, helping prompt his interest in Planck's hypothesis and subsequent work on quantum statistics.
shared_activities: early engagement with quantum theory in Calcutta
connections.notes: The relationship is documented as an important intellectual stimulus; the two men were distinct physicists despite their shared surname.

connections.relationship_description: Dirac named the class of integer-spin particles "bosons" in recognition of Bose's foundational contribution to quantum statistics.
shared_activities: development and interpretation of quantum statistics
connections.notes: This was principally an intellectual and commemorative connection rather than a documented close collaboration.

connections.relationship_description: Tagore dedicated his 1937 science book Visva-Parichay to Bose, recognizing Bose's standing in Bengal's scientific and intellectual life.
connections.notes: Bose was also well versed in Tagore's poetry and promoted Bengali as a language of scientific instruction.

category_summaries.summary: Bose's family supplied the durable personal setting behind a life divided between Calcutta, Dhaka, and European laboratories. His parents situated him in a railway-accountant household that valued education, while his 1914 marriage became a lifelong partnership and a large family household that endured alongside his academic career.

Bose's academic network began in Calcutta's unusually fertile institutional world. Presidency College teachers and the newly created University of Calcutta Science College gave a mathematically gifted student exposure to modern science, while later intellectual guidance and access to Planck's writings helped direct his attention toward the quantum questions that culminated in his 1924 breakthrough. These ties also illustrate the importance of locally built institutions to his emergence as a scientist.

Scientific collaboration turned Bose's local work into an international transformation of quantum theory. His sustained partnership with Saha introduced relativity to a wider Indian readership and produced joint research, but Einstein's 1924 intervention was the decisive catalytic tie: it placed Bose's paper in Zeitschrift für Physik, generated Bose-Einstein statistics, and opened the way to European laboratory work and leadership at Dhaka. Later recognition from figures such as Tagore and Dirac shows how Bose's influence extended beyond direct collaboration into Bengal's intellectual culture and the permanent vocabulary of particle physics.
